content: Psyllium seed husks, also referred to as ispaghula or simply psyllium, are derived from the seeds of the plant Plantago psyllium or Plantago ovata. These husks are known for their ability to expand and become mucilaginous when exposed to water. While they are soluble in water, they remain indigestible in humans. The husks are typically dried and then either chopped or powdered for use. They can be utilized as a standalone product or as an ingredient in various finished products. Psyllium seeds themselves are similar to the husks and can serve many of the same purposes, although they are less commonly used. When consumed, psyllium seed husks provide inert bulk, which helps maintain a consistent volume of solid material in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. This property makes them particularly useful for treatments aimed at improving or maintaining GI transit time, regardless of dietary variations or underlying gut conditions. Over-the-counter laxatives and fiber supplements, such as Metamucil, Serutan, Effersyllium, and Isabgol, often list psyllium husks as their primary ingredient, typically in finely chopped or powdered form. Alternatively, the husks can be consumed as-is, provided they are taken with sufficient water or other fluids to achieve the desired effect. Psyllium can also be incorporated into food or beverages to enhance dietary fiber intake. Certain cereals, such as Bran Buds and Heartwise, include psyllium as an ingredient. The husks are widely used to alleviate constipation, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), diverticular disease, and diarrhea. Additionally, they are employed as a regular dietary supplement to promote and maintain consistent GI transit. Emerging research suggests that psyllium may also play a role in lowering cholesterol levels and aiding in the management of diabetes.
